Other cells seem to contradict the matrix, and each one teaches something about reading data like
this.

- **The smash corner against Cover 2** succeeds only 49% of
  the time, below the chart's average. But a corner route is a 20-yard throw toward the sideline, caught
  about half the time against most coverages, and success rate counts every incompletion as a failure. The
  corner route's own average is 45%; against that baseline, Cover 2 is one
  of its better columns.
- **Slants and digs against Cover 3** succeed more often than average
  (61% and 58%), although four
  underneath defenders should make inside throws risky. Every route does a little better than its own
  average against Cover 3, the coverage that concedes underneath to protect against the deep ball, and
  a quarterback throws the slant against Cover 3 only after he has seen the hook defender leave its
  window. The cell records the result of a read, not of a call.
- **Crossers against man** (Cover 1 53%, Cover 0
  50%) succeed at about the crosser's usual rate, with no sign of
  mesh's double plus. The label lumps shallow crossers together with deep ones, and success rate calls
  a 6-yard catch on third-and-8 a failure however open the receiver was. It is also possible that the
  man-beater's edge is simply smaller than coaching lore says, which is this section's point.

Two cautions apply to every cell. First, the chart shows only the route *thrown to*, and the
quarterback chooses that route after seeing the coverage, so every cell is already the result of
someone's read. Second, success rate punishes deep routes, which fail more often and win bigger.
Neither caution changes the headline: **even the best matchups fail more than a third of the time.**
A coverage beater moves the odds by a few points per throw. That still matters. Over a season of
about 600 dropbacks, three points per throw is about 18 more successful plays, roughly one a game,
which is why coordinators spend their week on it ([The Game-Planning Week](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)).

### Calling against a menu, not a coverage

So a play-caller doesn't pick the beater for *the* coverage; he picks the concept with the best
expected result against the coverages this defense is likely to play in this situation. That is a
weighted average, and you can do it with the matrix. Suppose that on second-and-7, film study says a
defense plays Cover 3 35% of the time, Cover 1 25%, quarters 25% and Cover 2 15%. Score each grade as
a number from −2 to +2, weight it by how often the coverage comes, and add. (This treats ordinal
grades as if they were measurements: nobody knows that a "++" is exactly twice a "+". It is a
heuristic for organising a judgment, not a forecast of yards, and the ranking it produces matters
more than the decimals.)

| Concept | Cover 3 (35%) | Cover 1 (25%) | Quarters (25%) | Cover 2 (15%) | Expected grade | Worst case |
|:--------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Smash | +1 | −1 | 0 | +2 | +0.40 | −1 |
| Flood | +2 | −1 | +1 | +1 | **+0.85** | −1 |
| Mesh | 0 | +2 | 0 | 0 | +0.50 | 0 |
| Dagger | 0 | 0 | +2 | +1 | +0.65 | 0 |
| Four verticals | +2 | 0 | −1 | +1 | +0.60 | −1 |

: A play-caller's arithmetic: matrix grades weighted by a hypothetical defense's second-and-7 coverage mix. {#tbl-ev}

Flood wins on average, because the most common coverage is the one it beats. But notice the last
column. Flood is bad against man, and one snap in four is man. Mesh and dagger never go below
zero. If the down is third-and-7 and a bad play ends the drive, a careful coordinator may prefer the
call with no bad outcome to the one with the best average. That is the logic of the next section.

## Two-way concepts: an answer for man and an answer for zone

A **[two-way concept](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-way-concept)** has an answer built in for
both man and zone coverage, so it isn't a bad call whatever the defense plays. There are two ways to
build one. The routes themselves can work against both (crossing routes rub against man and settle
into holes against zone), or a receiver can change his route after the snap according to the
coverage, the [option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route) of
[Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), whose runner breaks
away from his defender against man and sits down in the window against zone. Mesh is the classic of
the first kind.

Notice what the two-way concept costs. Against zone, mesh's crossers are *fine*, settling for five or
six yards in front of defenders who rally to them; they are not a zone beater the way flood is. In the
matrix, mesh is grey across the zone columns: never bad, rarely great. That is the trade. A two-way
concept gives up some of the ceiling of a pure beater to raise the floor. On third-and-3, where five
or six yards is a first down and a bad call ends the drive, that is a bargain. On first-and-10, where a
coordinator can afford a swing for a big gain, he may prefer the pure beater and accept that it will
sometimes meet the wrong coverage.

There are three common ways offenses build two-way plays:

- **Routes that work against both.** Mesh, drive and the shallow cross rub against man and find holes
  against zone. So does a slant run inside a defender with outside leverage.
- **Choices inside one route.** The option route, a seam route that stays straight against one
  deep safety and bends into the open middle against two (a
  [route conversion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-conversion)), and the hitch that turns
  into a fade against press: each receiver reads the coverage after the snap, and the quarterback reads
  the same thing.
- **A man side and a zone side.** Put a zone beater on one half of the field (curl-flat, smash) and a
  man-beater on the other (a rub, a slant-flat), and let the quarterback choose his half from the
  man/zone read: the [man/zone indicator](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-zone-indicator) on a
  motion before the snap, or the corners' first steps after it. This is called a *half-field* or
  *combination* call, and many third-down playbooks are built from them.

All three ask more of the quarterback and the receivers than a single beater does, because now both
of them must read the coverage the same way, at speed. When they disagree, the result is the
interception where the receiver turned out and the ball went in. That is why two-way concepts are a
veteran offense's tool and why young quarterbacks are often given simpler, single-answer calls.

## The defense answers back

If the offense's job is to call the concept that beats the defense's coverage, the defense's job is to
play a coverage that beats the offense's concept, or at least doesn't lose to it. Defenses fight the
matrix in three ways.

**Change the coverage's rules against a known concept.** This is the match idea from Part 6 seen as a
counter. The clearest example is four verticals against Cover 3. Spot-drop Cover 3 loses to it by
arithmetic; Cover 3 match changes one rule, the seam-flat defender's, and the arithmetic is gone.

Match rules invite their own answers, and they are the counter-counters in the table below. A
seam-flat defender who carries #2 vertically is not in the flat, so the back or a quick out by #1 is
open underneath him. And route combinations that make two defenders' rules collide create holes that
no single rule covers. The cleanest is
[post-wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-wheel), and it is why that concept gets the only
"++" in the Cover 3 match column: #1 runs a post, and the corner, whose rule is to carry a vertical #1,
goes inside with him; #2 starts toward the flat, so the seam-flat defender, by rule, goes with him
underneath; then #2 turns up the sideline. The corner is inside, the seam-flat defender is trailing
from below, and nobody is over the top of the wheel. A **switch release** does something similar at the
snap: #1 and #2 cross, the outside receiver running inside and the slot outside, so the corner and the
seam-flat defender each have to decide in their first step who is now #1 and who is #2. If they
hesitate, or both take the same man, the other is free
([Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) draws both).

The same move, changing the rules, works against smash. Smash beats Cover 2 because the corner sits on
the hitch and the safety starts too far inside for the corner route. Palms keeps the two-high picture
but changes who covers whom on that side, and both defenders read #2. If #2 goes vertical, the safety
carries him, and the corner, freed of any deep worry, plays #1 man to man, which means sitting on
any short route by #1. If #2 instead breaks short to the flat, the corner jumps him and the safety
takes #1. Against smash, #2's corner route starts vertical, so the first rule applies.

::: {#cell-fig-smash-palms .cell execution_count=12}

Why does the matrix call smash "even" against quarters but a loss against Palms, if a vertical #2
makes Palms play like quarters? Because plain quarters handles smash in much the same way, which is
why that cell is grey, not blue. What Palms adds is the trap on the other branch: if the offense
answers with a quick out by #2, the corner, reading #2 from the start, jumps it.

**Take the beater's target away directly.** Brackets, robbers and lurkers put an extra defender where
a known concept wants to throw ([Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). A defense
that expects mesh on third-and-short can sit a linebacker at the mesh point, at five yards over the
ball, so the crossers run into him instead of past each other. A defense that expects dagger can rob
the dig with a safety who ignores the seam: usually the backside safety, freed when his own #2 stays
short, or a [poach](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-poach) call that sends him across on purpose.

**Make the coverage hard to identify.** Disguise and late rotation don't change the matrix; they hide
which column the offense is in until it's too late to use it. That is why a beater called before the
snap is a bet and a beater *chosen* after the snap, by a quarterback reading the key defender, is
much closer to a sure thing.

And the offense answers the answers. Every counter has a hole of its own, and the defense's counter
becomes the next concept's target:

| The defense's counter | What it takes away | What it opens | The offense's counter-counter |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------------------|
| Cover 3 match | four verticals | the flat and space behind carries | post-wheel; switch releases; the back to the flat |
| Palms | smash; quick outs by #2 | the corner jumping #2 | an out-and-up (an out that turns up the sideline) or wheel by #2; a [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) by #1 |
| Quarters poach, or a backside safety robbing | dagger; deep crossers | the backside receiver one-on-one | a backside vertical to hold the safety; throw to the isolated backside receiver |
| Tampa 2 | the seams between the safeties | the Mike's depth; the curl windows | read the Mike: throw the seam he didn't take; levels under him |
| Robber or lurk | in-cuts and crossers | the side he leaves | look him off; throw behind him |
| 2-Man | vertical stretches | out-breaking routes, the back, scrambles | quick outs; RB routes; designed quarterback runs |
| Fire zone | the hot throw | the seams; the window behind the dropper | seams; screens; throw over the dropper |

: Counters and counter-counters. Each answer creates the next question, which is why the matrix is never finished. {#tbl-counters}

Which side is ahead at any moment depends on who has the newer answer and the better players. That
back-and-forth over many plays, how a coordinator sets up one call with another, is the subject of
[Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other](08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd).

## The alert: calling the shot before the snap

One more pre-snap tool turns the coverage read into a big play. An
**[alert](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alert)** (many staffs say
[shot alert](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shot-alert)) is a pre-planned exception to the called
play: *if* the quarterback sees a particular look before the snap, he throws to the alert receiver
first, usually on a deep route; if he doesn't see it, he runs the play as called. The play-caller
builds it in; the quarterback decides at the line.

The classic trigger is a **single deep safety with the offense's best receiver isolated** on the
other side of the field, one-on-one against a corner with no help leaning his way. That is the
situation in which a deep throw has the best odds and the highest payoff: the receiver only has to
beat one man, and if he does, nobody is behind the corner. Other alerts are keyed to Cover 0 (any
one-on-one deep with no safety at all), to a pressed corner whose leverage gives away the throw (one
shaded inside with no deep help is conceding the fade or the back-shoulder throw outside; one shaded
outside with no inside help is conceding the slant), or to a safety cheating down into the box
against play-action. A [shot play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shot-play)
from [Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
is called *to* take a deep shot; an alert is a shot that the defense has to *give*.

Why not just call the deep shot? Because the deep shot is a bad play against most coverages and a
great one against a few, and the alert lets the offense take it only when the coverage shows that it
is one of the few. The called play underneath is the insurance. **What it costs** is that the
quarterback makes the decision before the snap, which is exactly the moment the defense is lying to
him. Alerts are therefore built around looks that are hard to fake: a single safety who can't get
back to the alert side in time, whatever he does at the snap, or a corner pressed with no help. If
the safety rotates over at the snap, a good quarterback abandons the alert and goes back to the play.

## Putting it together: identify, then predict

Everything above reduces to a routine you can run on any passing play, live or on the replay: the
quarterback's four steps, minus the throwing. Call the shell and your two likeliest coverages; watch
the safeties at the snap; let the corners name the coverage within its family; find the defender the
routes are putting in conflict (two receivers to one sideline at two depths means a high-low on that
side's corner or curl-flat defender; a slot running up the seam means somebody's rule about #2 is
being tested); then say the open receiver out loud before the ball is thrown. The checklist in
"Watch for it on Sunday" below is the pocket version.

The four animated plays in this chapter are drills for exactly this. Run them again (on the website
they are videos; in print, cover panels 3 and 4 with your hand) and, at panel 2, name the coverage and
the open receiver before you look.

## Film room

The famous concept-against-coverage plays have homes of their own in this book: the Chiefs'
"Jet Chip Wasp" on third-and-15 in Super Bowl LIV is drawn in
[Case Study: Andy Reid's Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd), and the Super Bowl XLIX
interception at the goal line, a rub concept met by a defense ready for it, in
[Case Study: Belichick's Patriots and the Game Plan](../12-case-studies/12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd).
Here are three more recent pictures of this chapter's ideas.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs, Super Bowls LVII and LVIII — the man-beater, and its counter"}
In Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023, the 2022 season) the Eagles played a lot of man coverage
against Kansas City, and two of the Chiefs' fourth-quarter touchdowns, the go-ahead score and the one
that followed it, came from the same idea. On both, a receiver went in motion across the formation and then, as the ball was snapped,
turned and ran back the way he had come. Kadarius Toney scored on the first; Skyy Moore on the second,
after his defender started across the formation with him. "As soon as I went in motion and I saw him
come in motion with me, I knew I had him," Moore said afterwards. Andy Reid's name for Toney's play
was "Corn Dog."[^corndog]

That is a man-beater in its purest form: it attacks the one thing man coverage must do, follow a
receiver, and uses the defender's own movement against him. A year later, in overtime of Super Bowl
LVIII (February 11, 2024), the Chiefs ran the same motion on first-and-goal from the 3-yard line. This time the call,
"Tom and Jerry," was built on the assumption that the 49ers would be ready for it. "We built corn dog
in saying, for sure they'll cover corn dog," Reid said. The first answer on the play was a shovel pass
to running back Jerick McKinnon underneath; when the 49ers converged on the shovel and played man on
the outside, Patrick Mahomes threw to Mecole Hardman, breaking back to the flat, for the
championship-winning touchdown.[^tomjerry]

**What to notice:** the play-caller designed for the defense's *counter* to the beater, not for the
beater itself. Note too that return motion only works against a defender who
[travels](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-travel-man-defender-follows-motion) with the motion man; a
defense that bumps, banjos or simply zones off the motion takes the edge away. On any goal-line snap,
watch the first defender to react to a motion. If he follows, it's man, and the motion man's turn back
is the throw.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — two-high, and what offenses could do about it"}
Mike Macdonald's 2025 Seahawks won Super Bowl LX playing more two-high coverage than any other playoff
team: from Week 14, when safety Julian Love returned to the lineup, through the Super Bowl, Next Gen
Stats counted split-safety coverage on 54.8% of their opponents' pass plays, and Seattle won all eight
of those games. Across the league, offenses converted 29.0% of dropbacks into first downs against
split-safety coverage in 2025, tied for the lowest rate since at least 2018.[^ngs-sea] (For a rough
comparison from a different charting source, FTN's 2025 labels in nflverse give a first-down rate of
29% against two-high and 34% against single-high
coverage.[^fdcalc])

**What to notice:** this is the matrix's quarters column in real life, and its Cover 6 column, which
plays quarters on one half. Against two-high, the concepts that work are the ones that make a read
safety pay for his rule (dagger, scissors, the quick out to #2) and, above all, the run, because two
safeties 12 yards deep leave a light box. The league noticed: in 2025, offenses used fewer than three
wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest share since Next Gen Stats began counting in
2016.[^heavy] Bigger personnel is partly a run-game answer to two-high coverage. When you watch a
two-high defense, count the run calls before you count the beaters.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Matthew Stafford, 2025 — the quarterback who beat two-high"}
Matthew Stafford won the 2025 MVP award with a league-leading 46 touchdown passes.[^stafford] In the
nflverse charting, he was also among the best quarterbacks in the league against two-high coverage:
on 249 dropbacks against Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6 he
averaged \+0\.26 expected points added per dropback, third
best of the 25 quarterbacks with at least 150 such dropbacks, against a league average
of \+0\.02.[^qbcalc]

**What to notice:** what a quarterback brings to the matrix. Two-high coverage is built to take away
the deep throw and the easy read; it is beaten by a quarterback who identifies the coverage at the
snap, moves a safety with his eyes and throws on time into a window between the levels: the dig
behind a read safety, the seam the Mike didn't carry. On a Rams passing down from 2025, watch
Stafford's helmet in the first second after the snap. It often goes where the ball isn't going.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Predict the open man.** For one quarter, on every dropback pass, make the coverage call and then a
prediction, before the ball is thrown.

- **Before the snap:** shell (one-high or two-high), corners (press or off), and the two coverages you
  think are most likely. Is a receiver isolated against a single safety? That's an alert candidate.
- **One second after the snap:** how many safeties in the middle? Then the corners: squat (Cover 2),
  bail (Cover 3), read (quarters), trail (man). Say the coverage out loud.
- **Name the conflict defender** on the side the routes are going: the corner (two receivers at two
  depths outside), the curl-flat defender (three at three levels), the read safety (a slot going up
  the seam), the matchup (crossers against man).
- **Predict the open receiver** from what that defender does, *before* the throw. Then watch.
- **Watch the quarterback's helmet.** Did he look one way and throw the other? Who moved?

**For your log:** coverage called, receiver predicted, receiver thrown to. Score yourself on the
predictions. Over a quarter you'll find that you get Cover 3 and Cover 2 right far more often than
quarters and match coverages, which is exactly the point of those coverages.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**This is the textbook alert: throw to X first.** One deep safety, already leaning toward the trips,
means X is one-on-one with no help on his side. The corner pressing him is shaded inside, so he is
taking away the slant and conceding the outside: the alert throw is a fade or a back-shoulder throw
up the left sideline. If X wins at the line, the throw has a high chance of a big gain, and the safety,
4 or 5 yards the wrong way and 14 deep, can't get there in time.

**The insurance:** if the safety rotates back toward X at the snap, or the corner bails off the press,
the alert is off and the quarterback works the flood to the trips side, where three receivers now
face a defense that has shifted its help that way. And the defense knows all of this: a single safety
cheating to trips is sometimes bait for exactly this throw, with a rotation back at the snap. That is
why an alert is decided before the snap but confirmed in the first half-second after it.
:::
:::

**What is the coverage, which defender should the quarterback read, and where will the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Tampa 2.** Two safeties splitting the field (middle open), corners squatting in the flats (Cover 2
corners), and the Mike running down the middle: that is the Tampa 2 Mike, whose job is to carry the
most dangerous seam and close the gap between the safeties that four verticals is built to hit.

**Read the Mike, then a safety.** The Mike can only carry one seam. Whichever he takes, the other seam
is a one-on-one high-low on that side's safety: the seam inside him and the go route outside him.
If the safety stays inside on the seam, the go route is open along the sideline behind the squatting
corner (the hole shot); if he widens toward the go route, as these two already have, the seam splits
the gap between him and the Mike. Here the Mike has opened toward Y's seam on the right, so the throw
is H's seam on the left, between the Mike and the free safety. This is where the look-off earns its
keep: a quarterback who wants that throw holds his eyes on Y's seam for a beat to keep the Mike
drifting right, and many offenses coach the seam runners to bend away from the Mike as well. If the
quarterback can't decide in time, the back underneath, past the two hook defenders who have dropped
deep under the verticals, is the checkdown. This is why four verticals is only a "+"
against Cover 2 in the matrix, not a "++": the Tampa Mike takes away half of the concept.
:::
:::

**You have four concepts on the call sheet: smash, flood, dagger and mesh. Using the matrix grades
(reprinted below), which has the best expected result? Which has the safest floor? Which would you
call, and why?**

| Concept | Cover 2 (30%) | Quarters (35%) | 2-Man (20%) | Cover 3 (15%) |
|:--------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Smash | +2 | 0 | −2 | +1 |
| Flood | +1 | +1 | −1 | +2 |
| Dagger | +1 | +2 | −1 | 0 |
| Mesh | 0 | 0 | +1 | 0 |

: The four rows of the matrix you need, with this defense's coverage mix. {#tbl-predict-call}

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Weight each grade by the coverage mix (Cover 2 30%, quarters 35%, 2-Man 20%, Cover 3 15%):

- **Smash:** +2, 0, −2, +1 → 0.60 + 0 − 0.40 + 0.15 = **+0.35**, worst case −2 (2-Man).
- **Flood:** +1, +1, −1, +2 → 0.30 + 0.35 − 0.20 + 0.30 = **+0.75**, worst case −1.
- **Dagger:** +1, +2, −1, 0 → 0.30 + 0.70 − 0.20 + 0 = **+0.80**, worst case −1.
- **Mesh:** 0, 0, +1, 0 → **+0.20**, worst case 0.

**Dagger has the best average**, because the most likely coverage, quarters, is the one it was built
to beat, and it is decent against Cover 2 too. Flood is a close second. Mesh never loses but rarely
wins big. Smash, the famous Cover 2 beater, is the worst choice here: this defense plays enough 2-Man
to punish it.

**What a coordinator would add.** Third-and-7 is a long-ish third down, and route depth matters as
much as the grade. Dagger's dig, at 15 or 16 yards, is past the sticks. Mesh's crossers settle at 5 or
6 yards against zone, short of the line to gain, so its "safe floor" is less safe than it looks: a
completed mesh crosser that is tackled a yard short still ends the drive. But dagger needs about three seconds, so the call depends on
the protection and on whether this defense blitzes on third down; against a pressure-heavy defense
the slightly quicker flood, or a two-way call, might be safer. And the 20% of 2-Man is the danger in every
choice except mesh: if the 2-Man share were higher, or the down shorter, mesh's floor would start to
look like the smart call. The matrix doesn't make the decision; it organises it.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **The quarterback reads coverage in four steps:** the shell before the snap (a hypothesis), the
  rotation at it (the middle open or closed one second later), the key defender after it (the one the
  concept puts in conflict), and the throw that defender leaves. The look-off is the same read run in
  reverse: move the key defender with your eyes, then throw where he was.
- **Every cell of the concept-by-coverage matrix follows from two questions:** where are this
  coverage's thin spots, and does it give help to the defender this concept attacks? Smash beats
  Cover 2 at the sideline; flood and four verticals beat Cover 3's arithmetic; dagger and scissors make
  quarters' read safeties pay for their rule; mesh beats man with traffic; quick throws, seams and
  screens beat pressure. Against split-field coverage, read each half on its own. The grid leaves out
  the run game, which is where Cover 3 and the two-high shells earn their keep.
- **Beaters are bets.** Disguise hides the coverage, match rules change what a label means, execution
  and talent widen or close windows, and the defense chooses by situation too. In charting data the
  edges are real but small: even the best route-against-coverage matchups fail more than a third of
  the time.
- **Two-way concepts trade ceiling for floor.** Built-in answers for man and for zone mean the call is
  never bad, at the cost of rarely being great; they rule third down.
- **The matrix is never finished.** Every defensive counter (Cover 3 match, Palms, Tampa 2, robbers)
  opens something new, and the offense's next concept attacks it. The shot alert lets the offense take
  a deep shot only when the coverage gives it.
- **Watching:** call the coverage one second after the snap, find the conflict defender, and predict
  the open man before the throw.
